content: The incentives provided to patients in these settings were likely of significant value, particularly for tuberculosis (TB) patients, even in higher-income countries. This is especially true in nations lacking robust social welfare systems, as TB is often associated with poverty. Studies reviewed indicated that material support was typically directed toward the most vulnerable groups, which likely contributed to improved health equity. However, if these incentives are not distributed equitably, they could exacerbate health disparities. The distribution and impact of material support are context-dependent and may vary both within and between countries. Patient education, including educational counseling, was analyzed through randomized controlled trials and observational studies. Patients who received education demonstrated better treatment success rates, higher treatment completion, improved cure rates, and better adherence to treatment protocols, with reduced rates of loss to follow-up. It is important to note that counseling in this context refers to educational counseling rather than psychological counseling. Patient education could be delivered orally or in written form by healthcare workers or pharmacists. It might occur as a one-time session at the end of the intensive therapy phase or during each follow-up visit. Educational sessions could involve only the healthcare worker or include the patient’s social network and family members. Ensuring that education and counseling are culturally appropriate is critical, and marginalized populations may require tailored educational efforts. Staff education interventions, including peer training, visual aids, decision-making tools, and laboratory staff education, were examined in both randomized controlled trials and observational studies. Improved staff education was associated with higher treatment success rates, slightly lower mortality rates, and reduced loss to follow-up. Enhanced staff education is likely to improve patient treatment outcomes and reduce stigma among healthcare workers by fostering a better understanding of TB and its treatment. Psychological support for TB patients varied and included self-help groups, alcohol cessation counseling, and TB clubs. Patients with access to psychological support had higher treatment completion and cure rates, as well as lower rates of treatment failure and loss to follow-up. However, concerns about confounding factors, such as illness severity in supported groups, and non-randomized allocation of patients to support groups were raised. Psychological support should be targeted at the most marginalized populations to maximize health equity. Subgroup analyses revealed that directly observed therapy (DOT) showed clear benefits for TB patients living with HIV, with significantly improved treatment outcomes. However, DOT may not be beneficial for all patients and is likely more effective in certain subgroups. Factors influencing treatment adherence and the need for DOT in other patient groups were not examined in the systematic review. Treatment adherence interventions are necessary, as treatment supervision alone is insufficient to ensure good TB treatment outcomes. Patient education should be provided to all TB patients, and additional adherence interventions should be tailored to individual patient needs, provider resources, and implementation conditions. For interventions involving telephone or video assistance, challenges such as reluctance to adopt new technology, privacy concerns, and telecommunication infrastructure limitations must be addressed. Collaboration with other medical service programs and governments may help fund and implement these interventions. Community-based or home-based DOT is generally more advantageous than health facility-based DOT. However, family members should not be the sole option for administering DOT. Trained lay providers or healthcare workers are better suited for communityor home-based DOT, though this approach may require additional healthcare workers and increased costs for staff time and travel. Combining lay providers and healthcare workers for DOT delivery is also an option. While communityor home-based DOT is more acceptable and accessible to patients, stigma may still be an issue, particularly if healthcare workers visit patients’ homes regularly. Careful analysis of family dynamics and training of family members providing DOT is essential, along with additional supervision by local supporters or healthcare workers. Healthcare workers must assess potential risk factors for poor adherence at the start of treatment to determine the most appropriate treatment administration option. Some patient groups, such as those with inflexible work or family responsibilities, may not be able to participate in DOT. Any treatment administration option must be accompanied by proper medical care, including regular TB drug pick-up, consultations with healthcare providers, free TB treatment, and essential information on TB treatment. Monitoring and evaluation of programs should measure whether incentives improve program performance. Decentralized care models for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) patients are recommended over centralized models. Decentralized care involves treatment and support provided in the patient’s local community by non-specialized health centers, community health workers, or volunteers. This approach improves treatment success and reduces loss to follow-up compared to centralized care. However, decentralized care may not be suitable for patients with severe TB, highly infectious forms of the disease, or serious co-morbidities. Measures to ensure patient safety, particularly for those on novel MDR-TB regimens, must be maintained in outpatient settings. National TB programs should establish standardized guidelines for determining patient eligibility for decentralized care. Patient preferences should be prioritized when choosing between centralized and decentralized care. Decentralized care requires appropriate treatment supervision, patient education, social support, staff training, infection control practices, and quality assurance. Cost considerations for decentralized care include faster treatment initiation and public health benefits, such as reducing TB transmission. However, legal barriers to decentralized care, particularly for treatments involving injections, must be addressed.
